author: Ollie South
excerpt: I rebuilt Bellingcat's donor-advised-fund total from free IRS filings. It comes back within 0.1 percent, but only on one reading of the years, and more than half of it sits in three rows paid to one charity in 2021.
title: Bellingcat's Donor-Fund Total Checks Out On One Reading Of The Years

author: T. Chaz Stevens, MSc, CLE Faculty
excerpt: Chaz Stevens asked the Broward Sheriff's Office for its payroll and got 3,100 sideways scans built to be unreadable. He shows how free tools turned them into a database, and how the numbers reached the governor's podium.
title: They Sent 3,100 Sideways Pages. The Data Was Still In There.

author: Dan Parks
excerpt: When an incident responder or security analyst receives a screenshot, the first response is to check it for tampering. However, even an authentic image capture can easily mask a fabricated chronological context. Cybersecurity professionals who manage extortion and leak-site claims should check the…
title: The Screenshot Is Real, But the Timeline Might Not Be

author: Tommy Two Times
excerpt: I checked every KEV entry since BOD 26-04 against CISA's own ratings. Thirteen that its table sends to forensic triage carry no flag, so I set my own trigger for collecting evidence before you patch.
title: CISA's Triage Flag Misses 13 Bugs Its Own Rules Say Need It
Building Appropriate And Defensible Security Programs

author: Adithya V
excerpt: Course samples are built to behave. Adithya V takes a live sample from MalwareBazaar, works it blind from strings to detonation, unmasks an infostealer, and owns up to what slipped past.
title: My First Real Malware Sample Turned Out To Be LokiBot

author: NetSniffer
excerpt: NASA's free fire map caught three earlier attacks on Borisoglebsk air base, faint fires included, and logged nothing after the October strike Ukraine says hit six Su-34s. What free heat and Sentinel-2 data can and can't say about the claims.
title: NASA's Fire Satellites Saw Nothing At Borisoglebsk This Time

author: Andy From Italy
excerpt: Taking a DoNex ransomware sample apart with the REA framework turns up a fatal flaw: it reuses one Salsa20 keystream for every file. The walkthrough builds a Python decryptor that uses a known-plaintext attack to strip the 512-byte footer and restore the files, with no key and no ransom paid.
title: Artificial Intelligence and Reverse Engineering: Defeating DoNex by Automating Analysis with REA and MCP Protocol

author: Ollie South
excerpt: UK company records now show whether directors and owners have proved who they are. What that verified label really tells you, what it leaves out, and how to check out a UK company for free.
title: What Companies House's New 'Verified' Label Proves, And What It Doesn't

author: NetSniffer
excerpt: AI video makers stamp their clips with hidden labels, but the copy of a war video you see has usually lost them. What each label is, what survives a repost, and an order of free checks for a clip you need to verify.
title: Why The Hidden Labels On AI War Videos Rarely Survive A Repost

author: Clara Whitlock
excerpt: A cyber incident at BAE Systems has stopped US bankruptcy courts mailing their notices since 9 October. Here is what is down, what still works, and what the courts' stopgap orders now expect lawyers, creditors and debtors to do themselves.
title: Bankruptcy Notices Are Down, And Courts Are Handing You The Job

author: Oliver Jones
excerpt: One prompt to an AWS AgentCore agent could unlock every other agent in the account region. AWS calls it expected and has since tightened the default role, but roles already deployed keep their old policy. The fix is in your account, not AWS's.
title: AgentCorruption: AWS Tightened AgentCore's Default Role, Not Yours

author: Tommy Two Times
excerpt: FortiManager lets one console run hundreds of Fortinet firewalls. Unit 42 has shown what happens when that console is breached: stolen keys, a hidden firewall implant, and why a 2024 patch did not end it. What to rotate and check on your FortiGates now.
title: PEERSTITCH: Why Patching FortiManager In 2024 Wasn't Enough

author: Clara Whitlock
excerpt: Microsoft has used a US court order to hit a marketplace and two kits behind a billion phishing messages. What the services were, why it is a civil seizure rather than an arrest, and what to check in your own Microsoft 365 tenant.
title: What Microsoft Actually Seized From YAM Store, CoGUI And Iron Man

author: Ollie South
excerpt: AI agents now do the legwork of open-source investigations and hand back answers with sources attached. Almost nobody has measured how often those sources are wrong. What the research shows, and a known-answer test you can run yourself.
title: How To Test An AI OSINT Agent Before You Trust Its Sources

author: NetSniffer
excerpt: Hundreds of trees came down on a public golf course in Washington, DC, and nobody agrees how many. What free satellite and aerial imagery can and cannot measure on a clearing like this, with a method you can repeat.
title: Why Satellites Can't Count The Trees Felled At East Potomac

author: Clara Whitlock
excerpt: Sextortion victims searching for help often found Digital Forensics Corporation, which promised to track down their blackmailer. The FTC says it faked the work, tracing a blackmailer from a link was never likely to work anyway, and the help that does work is free.
title: FTC Says A Sextortion Help Firm Faked Its Hunt For Blackmailers

author: Oliver Jones
excerpt: GitHub Copilot's agent in Visual Studio and SQL Server Management Studio was meant to be barred from editing its own settings. A trailing dot broke that rule, Microsoft has fixed it, and database teams may miss the patch.
title: A Single Dot Let Copilot Rewrite Its Own Rules In Visual Studio

author: Tommy Two Times
excerpt: Device code phishing gets attackers into Microsoft 365 accounts even when the victim signs in with a passkey. Why that is, and how to switch the device code flow off in Entra ID without breaking the few things that need it.
title: Passkeys Don't Stop Device Code Phishing. Blocking The Flow Does

author: Clara Whitlock
excerpt: Poland's prosecutors have published what government experts found inside the Pegasus spyware system the previous government used. Here is who really controlled it, what the findings do not prove, and the lesson for anyone running a tool its vendor still manages.
title: Poland Ran Pegasus Without Holding The Keys

author: Ollie South
excerpt: Volunteer OSINT teams scrape websites every day, often without asking whether the law allows it. Here is how US anti-hacking law, site terms and Europe's data protection rules each treat scraping, and a checklist for staying on the right side of all three.
title: Scraping Public Websites For OSINT: Where The Legal Risk Starts

author: NetSniffer
excerpt: Shadows can tell you when a photo was taken, but the standard method cannot say whether the sun was out, and it fits two dates a year. Here is how to close both gaps with free weather and satellite data, tested on a photo whose time we already know.
title: How To Date A Photo From Its Shadows, And Check The Sun Was Out

author: Clara Whitlock
excerpt: North Korean IT workers pose as remote staff at Western firms while paid Americans host their work laptops. The latest US arrests and Texas raids are two separate cases. Here is who was charged, how the scheme has changed and what to check.
title: North Korean IT Worker Raids: Who Was Charged, And With What

author: Oliver Jones
excerpt: MCP servers give AI agents their tools, and each one is code or a service you are trusting with your agent's permissions. Here is how to review one before you connect it, pin what you approved, and check it again after every update.
title: How To Vet An MCP Server Before Your AI Agent Uses It

author: Tommy Two Times
excerpt: Since September, the EU's Cyber Resilience Act has made product makers report attacks on their products within 24 hours, even for kit they no longer support. The hacked supermarket fridges in France show what that means and where the rule will be tested.
title: Europe's 24-Hour Hack Reporting Rule, Tested On France's Fridges

author: Ollie South
excerpt: The US has stopped collecting the names of the people who really own its companies. Here is what FinCEN's final rule changed, and the free records investigators can still use to put a name to an LLC.
title: Who Owns A US Company Now That FinCEN Has Stopped Asking

author: NetSniffer
excerpt: Investigators who follow sanctioned ships usually pay for tracking data. I replayed Bellingcat's investigation into the Russian cargo ship Patria with free tools only, to show which parts anyone can check and which still need a subscription.
title: Tracking A Sanctioned Russian Ship Using Only Free Data

author: Oliver Jones
excerpt: Security teams are handing log triage to AI assistants, but attackers write much of what is in those logs. How prompt injection reaches a SOC through its own evidence, what the research really measures, and which defences hold up.

author: Tommy Two Times
excerpt: Microsoft's October update fixed more than 1,400 security flaws, a record. Here is how to sort them by real risk using the four questions CISA now asks of every federal patch, and why one exploited bug outranks 76 critical ones.

author: Clara Whitlock
excerpt: The Secjuice weekly roundup for 12 to 16 October 2026: the exploited bugs to patch first, the takedowns and court cases worth knowing, and why each one matters to you, every item linked to its source.

title: How To Link Anonymous Websites To One Operator, With Free Tools

author: NetSniffer
excerpt: Satellite images settle arguments about wars and disasters, but their dates are often hidden or misread, and some are faked. How to date one with free tools, worked on Gaza's viral Google imagery, and which checks catch a doctored tile.
